subject: history_social
passage: Ancient merchant ships in the Mediterranean carried wine and olive oil in amphorae, clay jars whose shapes reveal what they held. Because sunken wrecks preserve these cargoes, archaeologists can use them to trace changes in trade. Studying wrecks found off the coast of southern France, archaeologist Giulia Ferri argues that between the first century BCE and the second century CE, olive oil did not merely join wine as a major cargo but displaced it: as oil cargoes became more common, wine cargoes became correspondingly rarer.

data.title: Wrecks off Southern France by Main Cargo

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Ferri's argument?

choices.A: More of the wrecks carried mainly olive oil than mainly wine in the second century CE.
choices.B: The total number of wrecks in each period stayed between about 50 and 60.
choices.C: From the first century BCE to the second century CE, wine wrecks fell from 48 to 14 as oil wrecks rose from 9 to 37.
choices.D: Wrecks carrying mainly olive oil outnumbered those carrying mainly wine in the first century CE, the middle period shown.

explanation.why: Ferri claims not just that oil became common but that it displaced wine: oil cargoes rose while wine cargoes fell. Support must show both columns changing in opposite directions over time. Wine wrecks fell from 48 to 14, while oil wrecks rose from 9 to 37.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This is true (37 versus 14), but a single period cannot show a change over time, let alone that wine declined as oil rose.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true (57, 53, and 51), but the total number of wrecks says nothing about which cargo was replacing which.
explanation.C: Correct. It shows wine cargoes declining while oil cargoes increased over the same span, which is the displacement Ferri describes.
explanation.D: Incorrect. In the first century CE, 31 wrecks carried mainly wine and 22 mainly oil, so this reverses the table.
